title: Language choice workshop
mission: Choose a language level for different projects and explain the benefits and drawbacks of each choice.
donow: Why might a school app and a small hardware routine need different language choices?
outcomes: Compare development effort at different language levels.
Justify language choices using project requirements.
starter: Which is usually easier for a person to understand: high-level source or binary machine code? Give a reason.
starter_answer: High-level source uses readable words and familiar operations. Binary machine code is harder for people to interpret.
terms: How readily a program can be used on another computer system.
How easily programmers can understand and change a program.

stations.name: Reading and changing code
facts: High-level code uses readable words and structures.
Readable code is usually easier to understand and change.
Low-level code requires more knowledge of the processor.
stations.challenge: Why might a high-level language help staff update a quiz each week?
stations.answer: Readable source is easier to understand, so staff can find and change the relevant parts.

tasks.q: Which priority most strongly supports high-level code for a changing school quiz?
a: Staff need to understand and edit it easily
Staff need binary instructions on paper
The code must never be translated
Every processor must share an instruction set
tasks.fb: Readability helps programmers maintain a frequently updated program.

tasks.q: Match the characteristic to its effect.
tasks.fb: A useful explanation connects a characteristic with its effect.

stations.info: Maintenance includes correcting and changing a program. High-level languages usually reduce the effort needed.

stations.name: Development time
facts: High-level operations can express a task in fewer instructions.
Low-level code often needs more detailed instructions.
More detailed code can take longer to write and check.
stations.challenge: Why can high-level code reduce development time?
stations.answer: One high-level operation can express work that needs several low-level instructions, reducing the code to write.

tasks.q: Why can high-level code be quicker to develop?
a: It can express a task with fewer instructions
It guarantees there are no errors
tasks.fb: Higher-level operations reduce the detail a programmer must write.

tasks.q: Select TWO reasonable comparisons.
opts: High-level code usually takes less effort to write
High-level code can never contain mistakes
Low-level code requires more processor detail
Low-level code is always easiest to maintain
correct: High-level code usually takes less effort to write
Low-level code requires more processor detail
tasks.fb: Compare typical characteristics without claiming that a language guarantees correctness.

stations.info: Development time is the time spent creating the program. It is different from the time the finished program takes to run.

stations.name: Moving to another system
facts: High-level source is usually more portable.
The new system needs a suitable translator.
Low-level code is tied more closely to a processor.
stations.challenge: Why may low-level code need rewriting for a different processor?
stations.answer: Its instructions are closely tied to one processor. Another processor may use a different instruction set.

tasks.q: Classify the language characteristic.
items: Usually easier to move between systems
Closely tied to a processor instruction set
Needs suitable translation on the new system
tasks.fb: High-level source is usually more portable, with a suitable translator.

tasks.q: What must be checked when moving high-level source to another system?
a: The keyboard has the same colour
tasks.fb: Portability still depends on translation support on the target system.

stations.info: Portability does not mean every source program works unchanged on every device. Compare the language levels using the requirement given.

stations.name: Control of hardware
facts: Low-level code closely matches processor operations.
It allows detailed control of hardware and memory use.
This control comes with greater development effort.
stations.challenge: Why might low-level code suit a routine needing precise hardware control?
stations.answer: Its instructions closely match processor operations, allowing the programmer to control hardware in detail.

tasks.q: Which requirement most strongly favours low-level code?
a: Readable code for weekly staff edits
Rapid writing of a general school app
tasks.fb: Low-level languages expose hardware operations in more detail.

tasks.q: Select TWO valid trade-offs.
opts: Low-level code can offer detailed hardware control
Low-level code is independent of every processor
Low-level code can be harder to maintain
Low-level code is always quickest to develop
correct: Low-level code can offer detailed hardware control
Low-level code can be harder to maintain
tasks.fb: Detailed control must be balanced against the effort needed to write and maintain the code.

stations.info: A strong answer explains why detailed hardware control matters to the stated task.

stations.name: Speed and memory
facts: Low-level code can be carefully tuned for a processor.
This can help control execution speed and memory use.
High-level code usually makes development easier.
stations.challenge: A tiny routine must use little memory. Give one benefit and one drawback of low-level code.
stations.answer: It allows detailed control of memory use, but can take longer to write and maintain.

tasks.q: Which benefit fits a routine with strict memory limits?
tasks.fb: Low-level code can give precise control, but it still uses memory.

tasks.q: Match each priority to the relevant characteristic.
tasks.fb: Choose a characteristic that directly addresses the requirement.

stations.info: Avoid claiming low-level code is always faster. Its relevant advantage is the detailed control it can give a programmer.

stations.name: A justified recommendation
facts: Identify the main requirement in the project.
Choose the language level that addresses it.
Explain both the benefit and a relevant drawback.
stations.challenge: Recommend a level for a school app that needs frequent changes on several systems.
stations.answer: High-level code is easier to maintain and usually more portable. Each system still needs suitable translation support.

tasks.q: Which recommendation best fits the school app?
a: High-level code supports readability and portability
Low-level code always runs on every system
Machine code is easiest for staff to read
tasks.fb: Link readability to updates and portability to use on different systems.

tasks.q: What drawback should accompany this recommendation?
a: The source still needs suitable translation
The source can never be changed
tasks.fb: A balanced recommendation includes the need for a suitable translator.

stations.info: Use the scenario to decide which characteristics matter. There is no single language level that is best for every task.

final.q: Choose a language level for each priority.
items: Easy weekly updates to a quiz
Quick development of a school app
Careful control of a tiny routine’s memory use
final.fb: Match readability and development speed to high-level code, and detailed hardware control to low-level code.

final.q: Match each choice to a relevant drawback.
pairs: High-level source on a new system
May need rewriting for another processor
Usually takes more effort to maintain
final.fb: Explain the trade-off, not just the choice.

final_answer: High-level: quiz updates and quick app development. Low-level: precise processor and memory control. Consider translation, portability and maintenance.
plenary: Explain two benefits of a high-level language for an app that needs regular updates on different systems. [4]
Readable source is easier to understand.
This makes regular changes easier.
High-level source is usually more portable.
It can be used on different systems with suitable translators.
A small routine needs precise hardware control. Explain one benefit and one drawback of low-level code. [4]
Its instructions closely match processor operations.
This allows detailed hardware control.
It requires more knowledge of the processor.
This can increase development effort.
Explain why portable high-level source still needs translation. [2]
A CPU cannot execute high-level source directly.
A suitable translator enables its instructions to be executed.

title: Translation studio
mission: Follow source code through translation and choose a compiler or interpreter for different working situations.
donow: Why can a CPU not simply follow a Python source file as written?
outcomes: Compare how compilers and interpreters work.
Justify a translator choice using the task requirements.
starter: A programmer writes total = price * quantity. Identify the source code and explain why the CPU needs another representation.
starter_answer: The written statement is source code. The CPU executes instructions in its own machine-code instruction set.
terms: A translator that processes a program into target code before that translated program runs.
Software that translates and executes source instructions as the program runs.

stations.name: Why translate?
facts: Source code expresses a program in a human-readable language.
A CPU executes compatible machine instructions.
A translator connects the source language to execution.
stations.challenge: Why is saving a source file not enough to make it executable by a CPU?
stations.answer: Saving keeps the source text. It does not itself translate the program into instructions the CPU can execute.

tasks.q: Why does high-level source need translation?
a: The CPU executes machine instructions, not high-level source directly
The CPU can only process images
tasks.fb: Translation changes representation. It does not prove the algorithm correct.

tasks.q: Match each item to its meaning.
pairs: Software that processes one code form into another
tasks.fb: Separate the program representation from the software that translates it.

stations.info: Compare the GCSE models: a compiler translates the whole source before execution, while an interpreter translates and executes one instruction at a time.

stations.name: The compiler route
facts: A compiler processes the source program before execution.
It reports translation errors it finds.
A successful build can produce code that is run later.
stations.challenge: Why might compilation suit software used repeatedly by customers?
stations.answer: Users can run the translated program repeatedly without translating the whole source again each time.

tasks.q: In the usual GCSE model, when does compilation happen?
a: Before the translated program is executed
Only after every run has finished
Only when the source is printed
tasks.fb: Compilation produces target code before that translated program runs.

tasks.q: Place each action in the build or run stage.
tasks.fb: A build creates translated code. Running executes it.

stations.info: Once a compiled executable exists, it can run again on a compatible system without translating the source again.

stations.name: The interpreter route
facts: An interpreter processes source instructions as they execute.
It typically stops when it encounters an error it cannot handle.
The usual GCSE model has no separate standalone executable.
stations.challenge: Why can an interpreter help during short edit-and-test cycles?
stations.answer: The programmer can edit source and test it without a separate whole-program compilation step.

tasks.q: Which best describes interpretation in the GCSE model?
a: Translate and execute instructions during the run
Translate the whole program once and discard the source
tasks.fb: Interpretation combines translation and execution during a run.

tasks.q: An unhandled error occurs during an interpreted run. What normally happens?
a: Execution stops and an error is reported
The source becomes machine code permanently
Every later instruction must still run
tasks.fb: Earlier instructions may already have run before the error is encountered.

stations.info: In the GCSE comparison, an interpreter translates and executes one instruction at a time. An error stops this process and provides feedback to the programmer.

stations.name: Error reporting
facts: A compiler reports errors found during translation.
An interpreter stops at an error as it processes the source.
Immediate feedback can help the programmer locate a problem.
stations.challenge: Why can an interpreter help a programmer locate an error during development?
stations.answer: It stops at the error it encounters and reports it, helping the programmer identify the source instruction to correct.

tasks.q: How can interpreter feedback help during development?
a: It identifies an error encountered during execution
It proves every output is correct
tasks.fb: Stopping and reporting an error helps the programmer locate the problem.

tasks.q: Match the error-reporting behaviour to the translator.
items: Stops at an error while processing source
May report several errors from a translation attempt
Earlier instructions may already have executed
tasks.fb: Compare when translation and execution happen.

stations.info: The programmer uses the error report to make a correction. A translator does not guarantee that a program produces the intended results.

stations.name: Running and distributing
facts: Compilation takes time before the first run.
Compiled code runs without repeating source translation.
Interpreted source needs translation each time it runs.
stations.challenge: Why can a compiled program run faster than interpreted source in the GCSE comparison?
stations.answer: Its source has already been translated, so execution does not repeatedly include source translation.

tasks.q: Select TWO compiler benefits.
opts: Translated code can be run again without source translation
Compilation removes every possible error
Users do not need the original compiler to run the executable
Compilation takes no time
correct: Translated code can be run again without source translation
Users do not need the original compiler to run the executable
tasks.fb: Compilation separates translation from running the resulting program.

tasks.q: Which is a drawback of interpretation in the GCSE comparison?
a: Repeated translation can make execution slower
It requires no source or interpreter
It always creates a standalone executable
tasks.fb: Translation takes place during each run, adding work during execution.

stations.info: These are the standard GCSE comparisons. A compiled executable must still be compatible with the system that runs it.

stations.name: Choosing a route
facts: Frequent edits can favour an interpreter during development.
Repeated distribution can favour a compiled build.
Give a reason linked to the stated requirement.
stations.challenge: Choose a route for a developer testing small changes frequently and explain your choice.
stations.answer: An interpreter supports quick edit-and-run cycles without a separate full compilation step.

tasks.q: A developer is testing many small changes. Which is a sound reason for using an interpreter?
a: It always hides the source code
It requires no software on the computer
tasks.fb: Link the choice to the work being done, not an absolute promise.

tasks.q: A team supplies a built application to users. Which compiler benefit fits?
a: Users can run the translated program without the original compiler
The program can never contain bugs
tasks.fb: The build separates translation from use. Compatibility and testing still matter.

stations.info: Many teams use both approaches in different parts of their workflow. A GCSE recommendation should use the requirements in the question.

final.q: Match each requirement to the translator benefit.
pairs: Interpreter stops and reports an error
Supply a program without its source
final.fb: Relate each benefit to how the translator works.

opts: Compilation takes place before the resulting program runs
An interpreter always produces a standalone executable
An interpreter translates during each run
A compiler guarantees correct outputs
correct: Compilation takes place before the resulting program runs
An interpreter translates during each run
final.fb: Compilation happens before execution of the result. Interpretation combines translation and execution.

final_answer: Interpreter: feedback during development. Compiler: repeated execution without source translation and distribution of an executable.
plenary: State why a high-level program needs a translator. [2]
The CPU executes machine code.
The translator processes high-level source into a form that can be executed.
Describe two differences between a compiler and an interpreter in the GCSE model. [4]
A compiler translates the source program before execution.
An interpreter translates and executes instructions during execution.
A compiled build can run again without retranslating the source each time.
Interpretation requires the interpreter or suitable runtime when running the source.
Explain one benefit and one drawback of using a compiler. [4]
The translated program can run without repeating source translation.
This can make execution faster than interpretation.
Compilation takes time before the program runs.
After a source change, the program must be compiled again.

title: IDE control room
mission: Explore the four main IDE facilities and explain how they help programmers write, translate and run programs.
donow: What help would you want from the software you use to write programs?
outcomes: Identify the four main IDE facilities.
Explain how each facility supports programming.
Use editing, diagnostics and execution tools in an IDE.
starter: A programmer needs to write source code and see its output. Name one tool for each job.
starter_answer: An editor is used to write the source. A run-time environment executes the program and lets the programmer view its output.
terms: An integrated development environment combines programming tools in one application.
Tools that report detected problems to help a programmer locate and correct them.

stations.name: Tools in one place
facts: An IDE combines programming facilities in one application.
Editors and diagnostics help create and correct source.
Translators and a run-time environment help execute it.
stations.challenge: How does an IDE help a programmer work on a program?
stations.answer: It brings tools for editing, diagnosing errors, translating and running together in one application.

tasks.q: What is an IDE?
tasks.fb: An IDE provides tools used while developing programs.

tasks.q: Match the facility to its role.
tasks.fb: The four facilities support different parts of development.

stations.info: An IDE combines these facilities so the programmer can work without repeatedly switching between separate applications.

stations.name: Writing source code
facts: Syntax highlighting uses colour to distinguish code elements.
Auto-completion suggests names or code as you type.
Indentation tools help present blocks clearly.
stations.challenge: How can auto-completion reduce mistakes without guaranteeing correct code?
stations.answer: It can reduce typing errors in suggested names, but the programmer can still select the wrong name or write the wrong logic.

tasks.q: Match the editor feature to the benefit.
pairs: Makes code elements easier to distinguish
tasks.fb: Editing support improves productivity and readability, but programmers still need to check their code.

tasks.q: Does syntax highlighting prove that a calculation is correct?
a: No, it mainly helps distinguish code elements
Yes, all coloured code is correct
Yes, if every line is blue
Only when the font is large
tasks.fb: Colour is a reading aid. It does not prove the algorithm gives the intended result.

stations.info: Colour meanings vary between themes and IDEs. Recognise what highlighting does rather than memorising one colour scheme.

stations.name: The run-time environment
facts: A run-time environment lets a programmer execute a program.
Input and output can be handled during the run.
The programmer can observe the program’s behaviour.
stations.challenge: What is the difference between the editor and the output area?
stations.answer: The editor contains the source being written. The output area shows what happens when the program runs.

tasks.q: Which facility runs the program so you can observe its output?
tasks.fb: The run-time environment supports execution and lets the programmer observe the result.

tasks.q: Where would you look to see the result of print(6 * 4)?
tasks.fb: The statement sends 24 to the output area.

stations.info: Use the Run control in your class IDE and find where it displays output. Names and layouts differ between IDEs.

stations.name: Diagnostic messages
facts: Diagnostics identify detected problems in the code.
A message can include a line number and an error description.
Read the surrounding code before deciding on a repair.
stations.challenge: A message points to line 5. Why might you also inspect line 4?
stations.answer: An earlier missing bracket or other error may only become apparent when the tool reaches the next line.

tasks.q: Which repair addresses the visible syntax error on line 4?
a: Add the closing ) after the string
tasks.fb: The opening bracket needs a matching closing bracket.

tasks.q: Select TWO sensible uses of diagnostics.
opts: Read the message to identify the kind of problem
Assume the IDE repairs every fault automatically
Inspect nearby lines as well as the highlighted one
Ignore testing once the message disappears
correct: Read the message to identify the kind of problem
Inspect nearby lines as well as the highlighted one
tasks.fb: Diagnostics guide investigation. The reported location may be where a problem was noticed.

stations.info: A warning can differ from an error that prevents execution. Read the message rather than treating every highlight as the same kind of problem.

stations.name: Translators in an IDE
facts: An IDE can use a compiler or an interpreter.
The translator processes the program’s source instructions.
Translation and execution have different roles.
stations.challenge: Why does an IDE need access to a translator for high-level source?
stations.answer: The CPU cannot execute high-level source directly. The translator enables the instructions to be executed.

tasks.q: What is the translator’s role in an IDE?
a: Process source into instructions that can be executed
tasks.fb: Translation enables high-level source to execute.

tasks.q: Match each facility with its action.
tasks.fb: Writing, translation and running are different jobs, even when one application provides them.

stations.info: The IDE may call a compiler or interpreter installed separately. The translator is a tool used by the IDE.

stations.name: Using your class IDE
facts: Open the IDE your teacher uses for programming.
Use its editor, Run control and output area.
Read a diagnostic message and correct its cause.
stations.challenge: In your class IDE, change a printed message and run it. Which two facilities did you use?
stations.answer: Use the editor to change the source. Use the run-time environment to execute it and view the new message.

tasks.q: Which action demonstrates using the editor?
a: Change a message in the source
tasks.fb: The editor is where the programmer writes and changes source.

tasks.q: A diagnostic reports a missing closing bracket. Which IDE facility lets you correct it?
tasks.fb: Read the diagnostic, then use the editor to correct the source.

stations.info: Practical task: in your class IDE, run print("Ready"), change the message and run it again. Remove the closing bracket, run to see the diagnostic, then restore it and rerun. Identify the translator used by the IDE. Record the IDE name and the facilities you used.

final.q: Choose the facility for each job.
pairs: Run the program and see output
final.fb: Explain what each facility does for the programmer.

final.q: After correcting source using a diagnostic, which facility lets you observe the new output?
final.fb: Execute the corrected program to see its output.

final_answer: Editor: change source. Error diagnostics: report problems. Translator: process source for execution. Run-time environment: execute and observe output.
plenary: Name two IDE editing facilities and explain how each helps a programmer. [4]
Syntax highlighting makes code elements easier to distinguish.
Auto-completion suggests names and can reduce typing errors.
Award one mark for each facility and one for its explained benefit.
Automatic indentation with a clear benefit is also acceptable.
Explain how an error diagnostic helps a programmer correct a problem. [2]
It can identify a location and describe the detected problem.
The programmer can use this information to find and correct the source.
Explain the roles of a translator and a run-time environment in an IDE. [4]
A translator processes high-level source instructions.
This enables instructions the CPU cannot execute directly to be executed.
A run-time environment runs the program.
It lets the programmer observe output and interact with the running program.

title: Language review HQ
mission: Apply the whole topic to short scenarios, check your reasoning and use review mode to repair misunderstandings.
donow: Which tool or language choice would most help you build a reliable revision app?
outcomes: Recall language levels and translator behaviour.
Select IDE tools for specific problems.
Write explanations linked to the needs of a scenario.
starter: A programmer wants readable source that is easy to update. Which language level usually suits this requirement, and why?
starter_answer: A high-level language usually suits it because readable words and structures make the code easier to understand and maintain.
terms: The program text written by a programmer before translation.
The facilities used to run a program and interact with it during execution.

stations.name: Language decisions
facts: High-level languages hide many hardware details.
Low-level languages expose processor operations.
The project requirements should guide the choice.
stations.challenge: Choose a level for a school app that needs frequent updates. Explain why.
stations.answer: High-level code is usually easier to read and maintain, helping staff update the app.

tasks.q: Choose the level that fits the priority.
tasks.fb: Link the language characteristic to the priority in the brief.

tasks.q: Why is “low-level is always better” a weak recommendation?
a: It ignores the requirements and development trade-offs
Every task needs machine code written by hand
tasks.fb: Different priorities lead to different language choices.

stations.info: A strong explanation names a characteristic and shows how it meets a requirement. A language name alone is often not enough.

stations.name: Source and execution
facts: Programmers write source code.
High-level source needs translation before the CPU can execute its instructions.
A CPU executes compatible machine code.
stations.challenge: Why can the CPU not execute a high-level source file directly?
stations.answer: Its instruction set uses machine code. The high-level source must be translated for its instructions to execute.

tasks.q: Match each description.
pairs: Program text written by a programmer
tasks.fb: Distinguish the program representation from the tool used to translate it.

tasks.q: Which representation does a compatible CPU execute directly?
tasks.fb: The CPU executes its machine instructions.

stations.info: Saving source code preserves the program text. It does not itself perform translation.

stations.name: Translator choices
facts: Compilers process source before the translated program runs.
Interpreters process source during execution.
Compiled code can run again without source translation.
stations.challenge: Which route supports quick testing of frequent source edits? Why?
stations.answer: An interpreter supports quick edit-and-run cycles without a separate whole-program compilation step.

tasks.q: Use the usual GCSE translator comparison.
items: Translate before executing the built program
Produce target code for later use
tasks.fb: Compilation translates before running the result. Interpretation translates during each run.

tasks.q: Which is a compiler benefit when distributing a finished program?
a: Users can run the executable without the original compiler
Every CPU can run any executable
The program can never contain an error
The original source must always be supplied
tasks.fb: A compiled executable separates running the program from translating its source.

stations.info: When comparing two approaches, make paired points. Explain what each does rather than listing unrelated advantages.

stations.name: Editing and diagnostics
facts: An editor lets a programmer write and change source.
Highlighting helps distinguish code elements.
Diagnostics describe detected problems.
stations.challenge: How do the editor and diagnostics work together when an error is reported?
stations.answer: The diagnostic helps locate and explain the problem. The programmer uses the editor to change the source.

tasks.q: Choose the tool for the job.
pairs: Suggest a variable name while typing
tasks.fb: Editing features support writing, while diagnostics help locate problems.

tasks.q: Which feature mainly makes keywords and strings easier to distinguish?
tasks.fb: Syntax highlighting changes the appearance of code elements.

stations.info: A diagnostic helps the programmer decide what to change. It does not guarantee an automatic repair.

stations.name: Translation and running
facts: An IDE can call a compiler or interpreter.
The run-time environment executes the program.
Input and output let the programmer interact with a run.
stations.challenge: Which IDE facility translates source, and which lets you observe a running program?
stations.answer: The translator processes the source. The run-time environment executes it and lets you observe output.

tasks.q: Which facility processes source instructions for execution?
tasks.fb: The translator processes source so its instructions can execute.

tasks.q: Which facility lets a programmer run a program and observe output?
tasks.fb: The run-time environment supports execution and interaction.

stations.info: Identify these facilities in your class IDE. The translator and run-time environment may work together behind a single Run button.

stations.name: Writing an explanation
facts: Read the programmer’s requirement.
Name a relevant language characteristic or IDE facility.
Explain how it helps in that situation.
stations.challenge: Improve “Use an IDE because it is good” for a programmer with a reported source error.
stations.answer: Error diagnostics can identify the problem and its location, helping the programmer find the source to correct.

tasks.q: Which response explains a relevant IDE benefit?
a: Diagnostics describe a problem and its location so the programmer can correct it
An IDE is good because it is modern
An IDE makes every program correct
tasks.fb: The explanation connects a specific facility to how it helps the programmer.

tasks.q: Select TWO useful parts of an explanation.
opts: Name the relevant facility
Only repeat the question
Link its benefit to the problem
Claim the IDE fixes every error
correct: Link its benefit to the problem
tasks.fb: Use a specific facility and explain its effect in the scenario.

stations.info: Use the available marks to judge how much explanation is needed. Accurate terminology and a clear link to the task matter.

pairs: Run the program and see output
final.fb: Link each choice to the requirement.

opts: Low-level code gives detailed hardware control
Every IDE automatically repairs every program
Compiled code can run again without source translation
High-level source executes directly on the CPU
correct: Low-level code gives detailed hardware control
Compiled code can run again without source translation
final.fb: Language characteristics and translator behaviour support different development needs.

final_answer: Frequent source edits: interpreter. Maintainable app: high-level language. Reported source problem: error diagnostics. Execution and output: run-time environment.
plenary: A school will update its quiz app each week. Explain two reasons for choosing a high-level language. [4]
Readable source helps staff understand the program.
This makes frequent changes easier to maintain.
Useful libraries can reduce how much code staff must write.
This can reduce development time for new features.
Compare a compiler and an interpreter. [4]
A compiler translates before the resulting program runs.
An interpreter processes source during execution.
Compiled target code can be run again without repeating source translation.
Interpreted source requires its interpreter or execution runtime.
Explain how an editor and error diagnostics help a programmer correct source code. [4]
Diagnostics describe a detected problem.
A reported location helps the programmer find it.
The editor lets the programmer change source text.
The programmer uses it to correct the identified instruction.
